summary: This informational document describes the interface primitives provided by UDP and UDP-Lite. It identifies the datagram services that these protocols expose to applications and how an application can configure and use their features.

plainLanguage.summary: It lists what simple, send-and-hope message services UDP offers and the knobs a program can adjust.

questions: how do i control udp ttl
subtitle: The settings and capabilities that UDP and UDP-Lite expose to applications

tldr.problem: UDP and UDP-Lite applications need to control low-level network behavior like TTL, checksums, and packet fragmentation, but the socket API has scattered options and missing documentation.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8304 inventories all the transport layer primitives (function calls and settings) that UDP and UDP-Lite provide to applications, organized by category: basic datagram operations, network layer controls, error reporting, and checksum handling.
tldr.outcome: This provides a complete reference for developers building applications with UDP and UDP-Lite, and serves as input to RFC 8303 (a broader guide on transport protocol features).

today: RFC 8304 is an Informational RFC that documents the transport features of UDP and UDP-Lite as they existed in 2018. It has not been obsoleted and remains a reference guide for the capabilities exposed by these protocols.

sections.title: UDP and UDP-Lite: Simple Message Services
sections.content:
UDP (User Datagram Protocol) and UDP-Lite (Lightweight UDP) are IETF Standards Track transport protocols that provide unidirectional, datagram-based communication. Unlike TCP, they send independent messages (datagrams) without establishing a connection, and they do not guarantee delivery or order.

UDP has been implemented and deployed for decades across the Internet. UDP-Lite is less common but useful for applications that can tolerate partially damaged payloads if they arrive faster than waiting for a retransmit. Both protocols expose many configuration options through the sockets API, allowing applications to control behavior at the IP layer (like TTL, checksums, and DSCP marking) that connection-oriented protocols like TCP normally manage themselves.

This document catalogs all these options—called primitives—so developers and the IETF can understand what UDP and UDP-Lite actually offer to applications.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP is a simple mail system: you write a postcard, drop it in the mailbox, and hope it arrives. But you can also adjust the mailbox's settings—like how far the postcard can travel, or whether to check it for damage.

sections.title: Core Datagram Primitives
sections.content:
The foundational primitives are CONNECT, SEND, RECEIVE, and CLOSE. Unlike TCP, UDP's CONNECT does not establish a connection or send any datagrams; it simply associates a remote address and port with a socket so the application can use shorthand SEND calls instead of specifying the destination each time. An application can RECEIVE from multiple sources on a single socket.

SEND passes the application's bytes to UDP for transmission as a single datagram. If the datagram cannot fit in an IP packet without fragmentation, the send fails. RECEIVE allocates a buffer and returns the data bytes along with the source address and port.

The CLOSE primitive terminates the socket. Since UDP is connectionless, this has only local significance; the remote endpoint is not notified.

Additional primitives include ERROR_REPORT, which informs the application of ICMP errors (such as port unreachable or packet too big), and is essential for implementations like path MTU discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: CONNECT says "I want to send to this address." SEND pushes a postcard out. RECEIVE waits for one to arrive with the sender's address. CLOSE throws away the mailbox.

sections.title: Network Layer Controls
sections.content:
UDP allows applications to configure IP-level behavior. SET_TTL and SET_IPV6_UNICAST_HOPS control the Time To Live (Hop Limit) field, limiting how many hops a datagram can traverse before being discarded. GET_TTL and GET_IPV6_UNICAST_HOPS read the TTL from incoming datagrams, useful for security checks.

SET_DF sets the Don't Fragment flag in IPv4 packets, preventing routers from fragmenting the datagram. Applications that care about path MTU discovery use this to probe the maximum packet size the network path supports.

SET_DSCP (and legacy ToS) marks the packet with a quality-of-service code point, letting the application request a service level (voice calls might request low latency; file transfer might use best effort). SET_ECN and GET_ECN manage Explicit Congestion Notification, allowing the application to respond to congestion signals without TCP's automatic response.

GET_MMS_S and GET_MMS_R return the maximum message size that can be sent or received on the configured interface without fragmentation.
sections.plainLanguage: SET_TTL says "don't let this postcard travel more than 64 hops." SET_DSCP says "this postcard is urgent, prioritize it." SET_DF says "if you can't fit this in one packet, don't bother fragmenting it."

sections.title: Checksum Control and Error Detection
sections.content:
CHECKSUM_ENABLED controls whether UDP computes a checksum on outgoing datagrams. By default, checksums are on; this primitive allows disabling them (useful for tunnels where the inner protocol has its own checksum). REQUIRE_CHECKSUM controls whether the receiver accepts datagrams with zero checksums; UDP defaults to requiring checksums.

SET_IP_OPTIONS and GET_IP_OPTIONS allow the application to send and receive IP options in the header, such as timestamps or specific routing directives.

For UDP-Lite specifically, the checksum covers only a portion of the payload, allowing partially damaged datagrams to be delivered. SET_CHECKSUM_COVERAGE tells the sender how many bytes of the datagram should be protected by the checksum; the remaining bytes are error-insensitive. SET_MIN_COVERAGE tells the receiver the minimum coverage it will accept, rejecting datagrams with less protection than required.
sections.plainLanguage: CHECKSUM_ENABLED says "include a damage check." For UDP-Lite, you can say "only check the first 100 bytes for damage; the rest is optional."

sections.title: Sockets API and Higher-Level Services
sections.content:
The sockets API is the IEEE standard for UDP access. Applications use calls like send(), sendto(), recv(), and recvfrom(), plus socket options (set via setsockopt()) to configure the primitives described above.

The POSIX API offers poll(), select(), and queue mechanisms for the application to be notified when data arrives or buffers are flushed. Some systems also support a callback-driven API built on top of these.

UDP-Lite is less widely deployed than UDP. Developers choosing between them should be aware that some network paths might not support UDP-Lite, forcing a fallback to UDP. RFC 8085 provides guidelines for UDP application design, including advice on handling packet loss, fragmentation, and congestion.
sections.plainLanguage: The sockets API is the standard way programs talk to UDP. You call send() to drop a postcard and recv() to wait for one. Socket options let you adjust the settings.

items.title: CONNECT
items.text: Set a default destination address and port (local operation only).

items.title: SEND
items.text: Transmit a datagram to the destination.

items.title: RECEIVE
items.text: Collect an arriving datagram with its source address.

items.title: ERROR_REPORT
items.text: Get ICMP errors like "unreachable" or "fragmentation needed."
